Checking & Savings Accounts Practical Ap: Finance Jigsaw Activity assessment by Charlie Han and Anthony Gee. Students should watch the opening video, use research, and apply checking/savings account concepts to realistic decisions. Suggested video: What's the Difference Between Checking & Savings? Kal Penn Explains | Mashable - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7K8pDRX3oaM

Collect student names or include the required name question below. Suggested Google Forms settings: make required questions required, turn on quiz mode if your teacher wants auto-scoring, and keep paragraph questions manually graded.

column8: Student provides first and last name.
column10: Use this for individual accountability because each student must turn in their own work.

column4: Enter your class period or teacher's requested identifier.
column10: Optional if Google Classroom already tracks section.

column4: Watch the opening video before answering: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7K8pDRX3oaM. In one complete sentence, write one difference between checking and savings accounts from the video.
column8: Response should identify a meaningful difference such as checking is for everyday spending and bills while savings is for storing money and earning interest.
column10: Manual grade for accuracy and complete sentence.

column3: What is the main purpose of a checking account?
column7: A place for everyday spending, debit card purchases, deposits, and bill payments | A long-term investment account for buying stocks | A loan that charges interest | Insurance that protects a car
column8: A place for everyday spending, debit card purchases, deposits, and bill payments

column3: What is the main purpose of a savings account?
column7: A place to separate money for goals or emergencies and possibly earn interest | A credit card account used to borrow money | A replacement for a paycheck | A way to avoid ever making a budget
column8: A place to separate money for goals or emergencies and possibly earn interest

column3: Which features should someone compare before opening a checking or savings account? Select all that apply.
column7: Monthly fees | Minimum balance requirements | ATM access and fees | APY or interest rate | Overdraft policy and fees | FDIC or NCUA insurance | The color of the debit card
column8: Monthly fees; Minimum balance requirements; ATM access and fees; APY or interest rate; Overdraft policy and fees; FDIC or NCUA insurance
column10: If Google Forms quiz mode is used, mark all correct except the debit card color option.

column4: You receive $250 from a weekend job. You owe a $48 phone bill this week, expect about $35 for food/transportation, and want to build emergency savings. How much would you leave in checking and how much would you move to savings? Defend your choice using at least two account features or risks.
column8: Strong answers keep enough in checking for near-term spending and move the rest to savings, while mentioning reasons such as avoiding overdrafts, separating savings from spending money, account fees, minimum balances, or emergency goals.
column10: Manual grade. There is not one exact split, but the reasoning must be realistic.

column3: Choose the better student checking account
column4: Bank A charges an $8 monthly fee unless you keep $500 in checking, has a $35 overdraft fee, and has only a few free ATMs. Bank B has no monthly fee, a large free ATM network, mobile deposit, and lets you turn overdraft coverage off. Which is usually better for a high school student with a small balance?
column7: Bank A | Bank B | They are exactly the same | Neither account can be used by students
column10: Follow-up explanation is in the next question.

column3: Explain your choice from the previous question
column4: Use evidence from the account details to explain why your choice is better for a student.
column8: Strong answers cite lower/no monthly fees, easier ATM access, mobile deposit, and lower overdraft risk as reasons Bank B is better for most students with small balances.

column4: You need to pay River City Utilities $42.75 on April 17, 2026 for a water bill. Write what belongs in each check field: Pay to the order of, numeric amount, written amount, and memo.
column8: Pay to the order of: River City Utilities; numeric amount: $42.75; written amount: Forty-two and 75/100 dollars; memo: water bill.
column10: Manual grade. Accept equivalent capitalization and date formatting.

column4: Starting checking balance: $185.40. Deposit: $62.00. Debit card purchase: $18.95. Check written: $42.75. ATM fee: $3.00. What is the ending balance?
Your transaction register says $182.70, but your banking app shows $225.45 because the $42.75 check has not cleared yet. What should you do before spending more money?
column8: Strong answers say not to treat the higher app balance as spendable, subtract outstanding checks/transactions, update the register, and avoid overdrawing the account.

column4: Find one real checking or savings account from a bank or credit union. Include the institution name, account name, monthly fee, minimum balance, APY or interest rate if listed, overdraft policy or fee if it is a checking account, and whether it is FDIC or NCUA insured. Paste the source link.
column8: Student provides a real researched account with required facts and a source link.
column10: This satisfies the research requirement. Manual grade for completeness and credible source.

column3: Would you recommend the account you researched?
column4: Would you recommend that account to a high school student? Explain your answer using at least three pieces of evidence from your research.
column8: Strong answers make a recommendation and support it with at least three facts such as fees, minimum balance, APY, ATM access, overdraft risk, insurance, or student-friendly features.
column10: Manual grade for critical thinking and evidence.

column4: After this activity, how confident are you that you can choose between a checking and savings account?
column8: Student selects a number from 1 to 5.
column10: Useful for lesson feedback, not assessment points.

column4: Write one habit you could use this month to manage checking or savings better.
column8: Student gives a realistic habit such as tracking transactions, setting a savings goal, avoiding overdrafts, checking fees, or reviewing statements.
